name: L'Rain
label: Mexican Summer
lede: Taja Cheek ran a radio station out of a pink Cadillac, booked a basement venue under her own apartment and curated at MoMA PS1, then took her mother's name for a band. Pitchfork gave her fourth record as L'Rain an 8.2.

eras.title: Ailey, Yale and Throw Vision
eras.text: Cheek grew up in Crown Heights studying ballet and modern dance at the Ailey School, then piano, cello and Baroque recorder, and bass last. Yale came with an American Studies degree, a Brooklyn band and a day job in the art world.

years.h: Yale's radio music director graduates in American Studies
years.p: Taja Cheek starts as a music major, runs the music desk at campus station WYBC, and graduates with distinction in American Studies.
years.xp:
Cheek had studied ballet and modern dance at the Ailey School as a kid, and picked up piano, cello and Baroque recorder before taking up bass in high school. At Yale she moved from music to American Studies, with a concentration built around visual, audio, literary and performance cultures.

Wikipedia lists her parents as Wyatt Cheek, a music marketing professional, and Lorraine C. Porter, an educator. Lorraine is where the stage name comes from.

years.src: Bedford + Bowery: Throw Vision · Wikipedia: L'Rain
years.h: Throw Vision forms as a trio in Brooklyn
years.p: Cheek plays keys in a band that blends jazz harmony, rock and ambient drift. A fourth member joins later.
years.xp:
Bedford + Bowery described a four-piece of Taja, Tiff, Alex and Dan in 2015: Cheek with classical piano and a jazz ear, one member trained in ethnomusicology, a classical percussionist new to rock bands, and a blues and improv guitarist. The trio formed in 2012, the fourth member came later.

Their limited clear-vinyl 7-inch, Were It Will, came out of songs worked up live, and the band played Palisades, the Knitting Factory and C'mon Everybody in Bed-Stuy that summer. Wikipedia dates a debut to 2013 and an EP to 2015.

eras.title: Radio from a pink Cadillac
eras.text: Cheek spends her twenties on the other side of the stage, producing art in public for Creative Time and programming outdoor shows at MoMA PS1, while a basement venue of her own gets going.

years.src: Wikipedia: L'Rain · Ben Sisto: JOB Interview
years.h: A working radio station in a pink Cadillac on Utica Avenue
years.p: As site manager of a Creative Time and Weeksville Heritage Center project, Cheek runs the station out of a parked Cadillac at the A/C stop in Bed-Stuy.
years.xp:
Cheek was a Creative Time fellow before she moved into curating, and she told Ben Sisto the job taught her grant writing and how the contemporary art world works. That same year she co-organized the Kara Walker project at the Domino Sugar Refinery with Ariana Allensworth, Salome Asega, Sable Elyse Smith and Nadia Williams.

Two years later she was at MoMA PS1, running the Sunday Sessions and Warm Up courtyard series. She kept the curator and musician sides deliberately apart in that period, she told Sisto.

years.src: Wikipedia: L'Rain · Ben Sisto: JOB Interview
years.p: Cheek opens the basement under her Brooklyn apartment to experimental shows, listed on Oh My Rockness, with co-organizers Max Alper, Dann Lawrence and Matteo Liberatore.
years.xp: Kyp Malone, Miho Hatori and Otomo Yoshihide have all played 49 Shade. According to Wikipedia, Bartees Strange has credited the room with connecting him to collaborators.

eras.title: A stage name from her mother
eras.text: The first L'Rain record comes out on a small Brooklyn label, under a name taken from Lorraine Porter, who died while it was being made.

years.h: L'Rain arrives, built from hundreds of field recordings
years.p: Cheek plays nearly everything on the debut, which comes out on Astro Nautico, and gets backing vocals from Kyp Malone of TV on the Radio.
years.xp:
Wikipedia lists Andrew Lappin on guitars and as co-producer, Alex Goldberg on drums and Jeremy Powell on saxophone. Pitchfork's Jay Balfour gave it 6.8 and called it a beautiful, untidy conduit for Cheek's emotional processing, per Wikipedia.

Pitchfork put it on its list of the 20 best experimental albums of 2017, and Bandcamp Daily ranked it #10 overall.

q: I realized after the first album was released that L'Rain was my mom's idea all along.
years.src: BOMB Magazine: Taja Cheek · Wikipedia: L'Rain (album)
years.h: Lorraine Porter, and the name that was hers
years.p: Cheek's mother died while the debut was being made. L'Rain is her name, pared down.
years.xp: The album cover is a photograph of the name tattooed on Cheek's forearm. Her mother had encouraged her to sing and play piano on her own, and Lappin, a friend, asked for a solo record after her band projects had dissolved.

years.h: Cheek remakes a 1980s Chicago house track for Bring Down the Walls
years.p: She, Morgan Wiley and Patrick Gordon redo "Your Love" for the compilation, which raised money for Critical Resistance, the prison-abolition group.
years.xp: The remake shows the other side of L'Rain: a dance-floor listener who is as at home with a house classic as with a field recording.

eras.title: Twenty players and a long sigh
eras.text: Fatigue lands on Mexican Summer with a cast of twenty and the critics' attention, and Cheek starts opening for bigger, stranger bands.

years.src: Wikipedia: Fatigue (album) · BOMB Magazine: Taja Cheek
years.h: Fatigue brings twenty players to Mexican Summer
years.p: Recorded in Brooklyn and at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles. "Find It" samples a pastor singing at a funeral Cheek attended.
years.xp:
She almost called it Suck Teeth, because she loved how it captured a very black sound of disapproval, annoyance and disappointment, according to Wikipedia. The phrase became a song instead. "Black Clap" uses sounds from a hand game she made with co-producer Ben Chapoteau-Katz.

Pitchfork gave it 8.5, per Wikipedia. The Wire named it album of the year, and Metacritic sits at 86/100. AllMusic called it bolder and dreamier than the debut.

years.src: BOMB Magazine: Taja Cheek · Wikipedia: L'Rain
years.h: Cheek opens for black midi and asks the crowd to sit
years.p: Her support sets start with the audience seated, a habit she described to BOMB.
years.xp: She told BOMB she often plays bars and dingy clubs and likes creating a bit of dissonance to transform them into somewhere else, using vocal loops, smudging and softness. Cheek's band at the time included Chapoteau-Katz, guitarist and bassist Justin Felton and drummer Alwyn Robinson.

yt: A Toes, Pitchfork Music Festival Chicago 2022 (fan-shot)
years.h: Animal Collective and Sharon Van Etten take her on the road
years.p: Cheek brings the looped, layered live show to two bigger names' rooms, and is listed as a former MoMA PS1 associate curator by July.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists her as a former associate curator at MoMA PS1 by July 2022. A fan-shot clip of her Pitchfork Music Festival set in Chicago that year is on YouTube.

eras.title: Bratty, diabolical, dad rock
eras.text: I Killed Your Dog is the loudest joke she has made, and the rooms get bigger.

years.h: Cheek calls I Killed Your Dog her bratty "anti-break-up" record
years.p: Her words for it: a bolder, brattier, more diabolical L'Rain, with indie dad rock folded into experimental electronics.
years.xp:
It was recorded across seven studios, including Abbey Road in London, Gary's Electric in Brooklyn and Wax Ltd in Hollywood. The singles were "New Year's UnResolution", "Pet Rock" (the video uses miniatures) and "r (Emote)".

Metacritic gave it 87/100, and Pitchfork named it Best New Music and ranked it 12th on its 2023 year-end list, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Celebrate Brooklyn! hands her its first artist-curator slot
years.p: BRIC's summer festival lets Cheek build the lineup, the same job she held at MoMA PS1.

years.h: Big Thief and LCD Soundsystem both put her on the bill
years.p: Cheek opens for the two bands in the year I Killed Your Dog comes out, per Wikipedia.

eras.title: Yes, and
eras.text: fata morgana is billed as the fourth and last part of a run that began in 2017, and the first to treat the experimental label as a limit.

years.big: "I was just noticing how people were treating my music with white gloves."
years.src: NPR: L'Rain's 'fata morgana' rewrites pop in her own image · Spectrum Culture: L'Rain: fata morgana
years.h: White gloves, and a ceiling Cheek wants to name
years.p: Cheek tells the New York Times how people around her handled her music. NPR hears the new record asking whether the barrier to pop is a glass ceiling or her own.
years.xp: NPR reads the album as Cheek asking whether the walls between her and mainstream pop are structural or self-imposed. It calls the result both alien and familiar, "yes/and" and not "either/or".

years.cap: L'Rain at Liberation Weekend, Washington, D.C.
years.src: The Fork: L'Rain fata morgana · Wikipedia: Fata Morgana (L'Rain album) · Paste: Review: L'Rain is in full control · Spectrum Culture: L'Rain: fata morgana
years.p: Stephen Kearse's review makes it Best New Music, Cheek's fourth record. "soulless cycle" leads on June 10, "borderline" follows July 8.
years.xp:
Cheek describes it as the last part of a continuum, the fourth record of a quadrilogy that revisits her mother's death, romantic ambiguity, exhaustion and looking for meaning in America now. It was made at Gary's Electric in Brooklyn with Ben Chapoteau-Katz and Andrew Lappin, and Welterweight Sound in Marlboro, NY, with sequencing by Yuka Honda.

The 13 tracks run about 39 minutes and take in dancehall, tape meditation, slow jams, gospel and crunched metal. Screechy Dan sings a dancehall outro on "july 5th". Paste gave it an A-, and Metacritic sits at 86/100. Lappin called the sound "craggy", per Spectrum Culture.
